ConsistencyGate: Preventing Memory Contamination in LLM Agents
via Self-Consistency Admission Control

Yan Zhang yz18b@fsu.edu Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, Florida State University    Shibo Li shiboli@cs.fsu.edu ††thanks: Corresponding author. Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, Florida State University
Abstract

LLM agents that operate over many turns accumulate facts in an external memory store and reuse them as premises for downstream reasoning. A hallucinated fact written at one step therefore persists as a false premise for every subsequent step, a failure mode we call memory contamination. Existing memory management addresses retrieval and capacity but not write-time correctness; this admission problem cannot be solved by utility- or recency-based criteria, and uncontrolled contamination compounds across long trajectories. We propose ConsistencyGate, a write-time admission gate that, before committing a candidate fact mm extracted from context cc, queries the LLM KK times for a soft support score and admits mm only when the average exceeds a threshold τ\tau. The mechanism is model-agnostic, requires no fine-tuning, and reduces to a single forward pass in a log-probability variant for latency-sensitive deployments. To measure the effect on natural data, we construct two real-conversation benchmarks (LoCoMo-Contam, MSC-Contam) by planting controlled single-detail corruptions in long-term conversations from LoCoMo and MSC, and complement them with a structured synthetic corpus (MemContam) that isolates a near-oracle upper bound. Across four LLM backbones, ConsistencyGate reduces contamination on every benchmark relative to a write-everything baseline, with the cost concentrated on facts that are stated only implicitly in the source context. We release all three benchmarks together with the gate implementation.

††firstpage: 1

1 Introduction

Long-horizon LLM agents accumulate facts in an external memory store and reason over them in later steps (Park et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024; Nakano et al., 2022). The architecture works only if the writer is reliable: a fact written once is read back many times, so any error introduced at write time becomes a false premise for every subsequent retrieval. Yet LLMs hallucinate even when extracting from a given context (Ji et al., 2023; Maynez et al., 2020; Manakul et al., 2023), so write-time errors are not rare. We study the resulting failure mode, which we call memory contamination: the accumulation of hallucinated facts in agent memory, and the way these errors compound over long interaction trajectories.

Memory contamination is distinct from the failure modes existing memory work addresses. It is not a retrieval problem: once a fact is stored, even an oracle retriever will surface it. It is not a capacity problem: contamination is not removed by eviction policies that rank candidates on utility rather than correctness. And it is not addressed by current admission policies, which score candidates on novelty, recency, or future utility (Zhang et al., 2026). A hallucinated fact such as Alice graduated in 2015 (when context says 2012) is as topically relevant, novel, and recent as the correct fact, so utility-based admission is structurally blind to contamination. Correctness is therefore an admission criterion that has no substitute in existing memory machinery.

We propose ConsistencyGate, a write-time admission gate that scores candidate facts on factual support rather than utility. Given a candidate fact mm extracted from context cc, the gate queries the LLM KK times with a verification prompt and averages a soft 0–1 support score; mm is admitted only when the average exceeds a threshold τ\tau. The mechanism is model-agnostic, requires no fine-tuning, and reduces to a single forward pass in a log-probability variant. The threshold τ\tau can be a fixed constant (we recommend τ=0.7\tau{=}0.7) or scheduled adaptively against memory occupancy when per-deployment tuning is infeasible.

To measure contamination on natural data, we construct LoCoMo-Contam and MSC-Contam from LoCoMo (Maharana et al., 2024) and MSC (Xu et al., 2022) by planting single-detail corruptions in probe facts. We complement these with MemContam, a synthetic benchmark whose unambiguous contexts isolate the gate’s behavior in a structured setting. Across the three benchmarks and four LLM backbones, ConsistencyGate consistently reduces contamination, with the cost concentrated on facts that are stated only implicitly in the source context.

Contributions.

(i) We characterize memory contamination as a write-time admission problem distinct from retrieval and capacity, and show that it compounds across interaction trajectories (§3). (ii) We propose ConsistencyGate, a soft-scoring admission criterion that admits a candidate fact only when its average support score across KK samples exceeds a threshold τ\tau; the criterion has two efficiency modes (KK-sample default and a single-pass log-probability variant) and a deployment fallback (a memory-occupancy-scaled threshold) when per-deployment tuning is infeasible (§4). (iii) We construct three benchmarks: MemContam (synthetic), LoCoMo-Contam, and MSC-Contam; to our knowledge the latter two are the first real-conversation corpora with planted, controllable contamination (§5). All three are released. (iv) On the real-conversation benchmarks, ConsistencyGate reduces contamination by 31.8% and 26.6% and lifts admission precision by 0.159 and 0.133 points on Qwen2.5-32B, with consistent gains across three additional LLM backbones; on MemContam it reaches a near-oracle 1.2% contamination at 100% recall (§6).

2 Background and Related Work

Memory in LLM agents.

External memory is a central component of long-horizon LLM agents (Park et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023; Weng, 2023), with episodic stores for conversation history (Zhong et al., 2023; Packer et al., 2024), semantic stores for extracted facts (Hu et al., 2023), and procedural stores for learned skills (Wang et al., 2024). We target the write process common to all three. Prior memory management has focused on retrieval (which stored memories to surface for a given query (Lewis et al., 2020; Gao et al., 2024)) and capacity control (what to evict when memory is full). The closest prior work is A-MAC (Zhang et al., 2026), which formalizes admission as a separate gate and scores candidate writes by a learned utility (novelty, recency, projected retrieval value). A-MAC’s objective is marginal usefulness; ConsistencyGate’s is factual support against the source context, and the two are not interchangeable: a correct fact and its hallucinated paraphrase have nearly identical utility but opposite correctness scores. The two gates are therefore complementary rather than competing (§3.2).

Hallucination detection and correction.

LLM hallucination is widely documented (Ji et al., 2023; Bang et al., 2023; Maynez et al., 2020), and a large literature aims to detect or repair it. Reference-free signals include atomic-fact decomposition with external evidence (FactScore, Min et al., 2023), calibration via the model’s own answer probabilities (Kadavath et al., 2022), and self-feedback rewriting (Self-Refine, Madaan et al., 2023; Chain-of-Verification, Dhuliawala et al., 2023; RARR, Gao et al., 2023). Retrieval-augmented variants such as Self-RAG (Asai et al., 2024) and CRAG (Yan et al., 2024) insert validity checks between retrieval and generation. ConsistencyGate sits at a different stage of the pipeline: rather than verifying a generated answer or filtering retrieved evidence, it gates writes into long-term memory before any downstream retrieval can amplify them. The closest point of contact is SelfCheckGPT (Manakul et al., 2023), which detects hallucination in generated text by sampling multiple outputs and measuring inter-sample agreement.

Self-consistency as a verification signal.

Wang et al. (2023) show that majority-vote aggregation over multiple reasoning chains improves reasoning accuracy because correct answers are more stable across samples than hallucinated ones. We adapt this principle to write-time memory admission: the gate queries the LLM KK times and admits a candidate fact only when the average support score exceeds a threshold. The key difference from the prior self-consistency line is that the source context cc is available at admission time, so the verifier grounds its judgment on a known evidence chunk rather than on the model’s prior alone.

3 Problem Setup

3.1 Notation

Let ℳ={(mi,ti)}\mathcal{M}=\{(m_{i},t_{i})\} denote an agent’s memory store, where mim_{i} is a text-form fact and tit_{i} is its timestamp. At each step tt, the agent observes context ctc_{t} (a conversation turn, a document chunk, or a tool output), and a memory writer 𝒲\mathcal{W} extracts a set of candidate facts ℱt=𝒲⁡(ct)\mathcal{F}_{t}=\mathcal{W}(c_{t}). A memory gate g:ℱt×ct→{0,1}|ℱt|g:\mathcal{F}_{t}\times c_{t}\to\{0,1\}^{|\mathcal{F}_{t}|} decides which facts to admit; admitted facts are appended to ℳ\mathcal{M}.

We measure memory contamination rate:

ρ=|{m∈ℳ:Verify​(m)=False}||ℳ|,\rho\;=\;\frac{|\{m\in\mathcal{M}:\text{Verify}(m)=\text{False}\}|}{|\mathcal{M}|}, (1)

where Verify​(m)\text{Verify}(m) returns the gold-label correctness of mm against its source context. In our three benchmarks Verify is provided by the construction protocol (§5); in deployment it would be approximated by audit or human review. Admission precision is 1−ρ1-\rho; admission recall is the fraction of correct candidates that the gate admits.

3.2 Contamination Rates and Downstream Cost

Under the WriteAll baseline (g≡1g\equiv 1), ρ=50%\rho=50\% on all three contaminated benchmarks (by construction), and downstream QA F1 collapses to 0.474 on MemContam, 0.227 on LoCoMo-Contam, and 0.338 on MSC-Contam (Table 1). The degradation is mechanistic: contaminated facts are retrieved alongside correct ones and injected as evidence into the answer prompt, so any retriever that does its job propagates the contamination.

Contamination cascades over a trajectory.

Write-time contamination compounds with interaction length. Once a hallucinated fact enters memory, an oracle retriever will still surface it; as memory fills, the fraction of contaminated retrievals grows and downstream answers depend more on false premises. We call this the contamination cascade and quantify it in Figure 2 (§6): an admission error at turn tt continues to corrupt turns t+1,t+2,…t{+}1,t{+}2,\ldots for the rest of the trajectory.

Utility-based admission cannot fix this.

A hallucinated fact (e.g.,“Alice graduated in 2015” when context says 2012) is as topically relevant, novel, and recent as the correct fact, so utility-based criteria (relevance scoring, novelty filtering, recency management) are structurally blind to contamination. The remedy is to score candidates on whether the source context supports them, which is the criterion ConsistencyGate operationalizes in §4.

4 ConsistencyGate: Self-Consistency Memory Admission

4.1 Core Algorithm

ConsistencyGate wraps any existing memory writer with a consistency-checking gate. Given a candidate fact mm extracted from context cc, we score mm’s reliability by querying the LLM KK times with a soft verification prompt that asks the model to rate how strongly mm is supported by cc on a continuous 0–1 scale (exact prompt in Appendix C):

sk=ℒ(prompt(m,c))∈[0,1],k=1,…,K,s_{k}=\mathcal{L}\bigl(\text{prompt}(m,c)\bigr)\in[0,1],\quad k=1,\ldots,K, (2)

where sk=1s_{k}=1 means fully supported, sk=0s_{k}=0 means contradicted, and sk=0.5s_{k}=0.5 means ambiguous. The consistency score is the average support across KK samples,

p^​(m∣c)=1K​∑k=1Ksk,\hat{p}(m\mid c)=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}s_{k}, (3)

and the admission decision is g(m,c)=𝟏[p^(m∣c)≥τ]g(m,c)=\mathbf{1}[\hat{p}(m\mid c)\geq\tau]. Algorithm 1 gives the full procedure. We recommend the fixed setting τ=0.7\tau{=}0.7, K=5K{=}5 as a default (see §6.5), with the adaptive schedule of §4.3 as a zero-tuning fallback.

4.2 Efficient Single-Pass Approximation

The default soft-scoring implementation issues KK LLM calls per candidate fact, which becomes expensive when the writer extracts many facts per context. We provide an alternative that uses token-level log-probabilities: switch to a binary yes/no prompt and read the score from a single forward pass,

p^log​(m∣c)=softmax⁡([log⁡p⁡(yes∣prompt),log⁡p⁡(no∣prompt)])​[0],\hat{p}_{\log}(m\mid c)=\mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\bigl[\log p(\texttt{yes}\mid\text{prompt}),\;\log p(\texttt{no}\mid\text{prompt})\bigr]\right)\!\bigl[0\bigr], (4)

which is exposed by most LLM serving stacks. The variant runs in 23–28 ms per fact across our four backbones (versus 264–363 ms at K=5K{=}5, a 12−14×12{-}14\times speedup) and matches or beats soft scoring on structured contexts. We name this asymmetry the bimodality of yes/no support: on structured contexts the model’s yes/no token probabilities saturate (log⁡P⁡(yes∣c,m+)→0\log P(\text{yes}\mid c,m_{+})\to 0 for correct m+m_{+}, log⁡P⁡(no∣c,m−)→0\log P(\text{no}\mid c,m_{-})\to 0 for corrupted m−m_{-}), so p^log\hat{p}_{\log} approximates p^\hat{p} in a single forward pass; on long-form conversational contexts the bimodal assumption breaks down and KK-sample averaging recovers an estimate that one logprob query cannot (Section 7).

4.3 Adaptive Thresholding

When τ\tau cannot be tuned for a particular model or deployment, we provide an adaptive schedule that scales the threshold with memory utilization:

τ∗​(|ℳ|,C,τmin,τmax)=τmin+(τmax−τmin)⋅|ℳ|C,\tau^{*}(|\mathcal{M}|,C;\tau_{\min},\tau_{\max})=\tau_{\min}+(\tau_{\max}-\tau_{\min})\cdot\frac{|\mathcal{M}|}{C}, (5)

where CC is the memory capacity, τmin\tau_{\min} is the floor at empty memory, and τmax\tau_{\max} the ceiling at full capacity. The schedule is monotone in occupancy: more permissive when memory is sparse, and stricter as memory fills. When the operating point can be tuned for the deployment, fixed τ=0.7\tau{=}0.7 outperforms the adaptive schedule (§6.5); the adaptive variant is recommended only when per-deployment tuning is infeasible.

5 Benchmarks

Existing memory benchmarks (Maharana et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2022) lack gold labels for fact-level accuracy, making it difficult to measure contamination rates precisely. We introduce three complementary benchmarks: a controlled synthetic corpus (MemContam) and two real-conversation corpora derived from existing long-term dialogue datasets (LoCoMo-Contam, MSC-Contam). All three impose a controlled 50% contamination rate so that the contamination metric is comparable across them.

Evaluation metrics (shared across benchmarks).

We report: (1) Contamination rate ρ\rho (% incorrect among admitted facts, lower is better); (2) Admission precision (% correct among admitted; equal to 1−ρ1-\rho); (3) Admission recall (% of correct facts admitted); and (4) Downstream QA F1 on question-answer pairs answerable from the correct facts.

5.1 MemContam (Synthetic)

Construction.

We define five fixed source contexts spanning diverse domains (personal biography, library record, recipe, science fair report, spacecraft mission log). Each context is used to generate 40 independent samples via Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, yielding 200 samples in total with broad lexical variation despite shared underlying entities. For each sample, the LLM extracts F=5F=5 ground-truth facts and generates F′=5F^{\prime}=5 plausible but incorrect variants using four corruption strategies: (a) numerical perturbation, (b) negation, (c) proper-noun substitution, and (d) appended contradicting clause. The benchmark contains 1,000 correct and 1,000 incorrect facts across the 200 contexts, yielding the controlled 50% contamination setting. Because corruption (d) appends a literal contradicting clause and the verifier shares a model family with the corpus generator, we treat MemContam results as an internal-consistency upper bound rather than a deployment headline; deployment-relevant numbers come from LoCoMo-Contam and MSC-Contam.

5.2 LoCoMo-Contam (Real Long-Term Conversations)

Source data.

LoCoMo-Contam is built on top of LoCoMo-10 (Maharana et al., 2024), a set of 10 long-term dyadic conversations (400–700 turns each, 19–32 sessions per conversation).

Construction.

For each of the 10 conversations we select up to N=5N{=}5 QA pairs whose answers are concrete and verifiable (factual or temporal categories). Each QA pair is converted into a self-contained fact statement using Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct (e.g.,“Caroline moved from Sweden 4 years ago.”), and a corrupted version is generated by prompting the model to change exactly one concrete detail to a plausible but incorrect alternative (e.g.,“Caroline moved from Germany 4 years ago.”). Both versions are then paraphrased into natural conversational turns as if spoken by one of the participants. The resulting benchmark contains 50 probe pairs (5 per conversation) at 50% contamination.

Evaluation protocol.

The agent first processes the full conversation to populate memory. Correct probe facts are then pre-seeded directly into memory (bypassing the gate) to ensure that retrieval evidence is always available; this design choice means downstream QA is insensitive to gate decisions on probe turns, so the primary signals on this benchmark are the contamination rate and admission precision (§6). Each probe turn (correct and corrupted) is then presented through the full observe pipeline: the memory writer extracts a fact, the gate queries memory for supporting context, and an admission decision is recorded. This tests whether the gate can distinguish a claim consistent with established memory from one that contradicts it, on real conversational data.

5.3 MSC-Contam (Persona-Grounded Conversations)

Source data.

MSC-Contam is built on top of the Multi-Session Chat dataset (Xu et al., 2022), a corpus of dyadic conversations grounded in evolving speaker personas (20 conversations, 2 sessions each).

Construction.

Unlike LoCoMo, MSC does not come with pre-annotated QA pairs; each speaker is instead seeded with a set of persona sentences at the start of each session. We filter persona sentences for concreteness (e.g.,“I have worked as a nurse for 10 years” vs. “I enjoy being outdoors”), keeping only those with a verifiable concrete detail (name, number, place, or occupation), and select up to N=5N{=}5 persona facts per conversation. For each fact, we generate a corrupted version by changing exactly one concrete detail to a plausible but incorrect alternative, using the same corruption prompts as LoCoMo-Contam. Both versions are then converted into natural conversational utterances, and QA pairs for downstream evaluation are generated directly from the original persona facts. The resulting benchmark contains 41 probe pairs (up to 5 per conversation ×\times 20 conversations; some conversations contain fewer than 5 concrete persona facts) at the same 50% contamination rate.

Evaluation protocol.

Identical to LoCoMo-Contam: the agent processes all session turns to populate memory, correct facts are pre-seeded, and each probe turn (correct and corrupted) is evaluated through the full gate pipeline. MSC-Contam differs from LoCoMo-Contam in that its sessions are shorter and more topically focused, and probe facts are persona-grounded rather than scattered across many conversational turns; this lets us test whether the gate can leverage persona memory established across multiple sessions.

6 Experiments

6.1 Experimental Setup

All agents use Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct (bfloat16, served via vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) on a single high-memory GPU sufficient for 32B-parameter serving) with sentence-transformer retrieval over a flat memory store; the memory writer extracts atomic facts in one pass per context chunk. MemContam evaluates the gate directly on gold candidate facts (bypassing the extraction step) to isolate admission accuracy; LoCoMo-Contam and MSC-Contam run the full agent pipeline. We compare two baselines: WriteAll (admits every fact) and Random (admits each fact with probability p=0.6p{=}0.6, matched to ConsistencyGate’s empirical admission rate at τ=0.7\tau{=}0.7 to isolate the contribution of correctness-based filtering from any reduction in memory size). ConsistencyGate uses our recommended configuration of fixed threshold τ=0.7\tau{=}0.7 with K=5K{=}5 samples and capacity C=500C{=}500 (chosen larger than the maximum candidate count per trajectory so capacity does not bind in any reported run); the adaptive threshold schedule and the single-pass LogProb variant are evaluated separately in §6.5. Cross-model experiments on Llama-3.3-70B and Llama4-Scout-17B-16E use two high-memory GPUs in tensor-parallel mode.

LLM use disclosure.

The LLM plays three roles: verifier inside ConsistencyGate, memory writer (candidate extraction), and corpus/corruption generator for benchmark construction (§5); the verifier and writer use whichever backbone is under evaluation, while the generator uses Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct only.

6.2 Main Results

Table 1 shows our main results across all four benchmarks (MemContam over 3 seeds).

MemContam.

On the synthetic benchmark, ConsistencyGate reduces contamination from 50.0% to 1.2% (a 97.6% relative reduction) at 100% recall of correct facts, and lifts downstream QA F1 from 0.474 to 0.840. We read this number as a near-oracle upper bound rather than a deployment number: MemContam contexts are short, factually unambiguous, and the corruption strategies leave differences large enough that a same-family LLM verifier resolves them with very few samples (see §7). The Random baseline does not improve over WriteAll, ruling out the explanation that any selective admission helps.

LoCoMo-Contam and MSC-Contam.

On real long-term conversations with planted corruptions, ConsistencyGate reduces contamination from 50.0% to 34.1% on LoCoMo-Contam (precision 0.500→0.6590.500{\to}0.659) and to 36.7% on MSC-Contam (precision 0.500→0.6330.500{\to}0.633); QA F1 is nearly unchanged because pre-seeding correct facts makes downstream QA insensitive to gate decisions on probe turns (§5.2). Recall on LoCoMo-Contam is 0.58 (systematic across all four backbones, range 0.52–0.68; Section 6.3) versus 0.93 on MSC-Contam: persona facts are stated explicitly and self-contained, whereas LoCoMo facts are often implicit or distributed across many turns and the verifier prompt requires support to be explicit. The deployment-side trade-off is discussed in §7 and §Limitations.

LoCoMo (clean).

On clean conversations ConsistencyGate reaches QA F1 =0.267=0.267 versus 0.271 for WriteAll (−1.5%-1.5\%); Random filtering at a comparable admission rate is substantially worse (F1 =0.227=0.227), indicating that the gain on contaminated data comes from correctness-based filtering rather than from any reduction in memory size.

6.3 Cross-Model Generalization

Table 2 reports ConsistencyGate on three additional backbones. On MemContam all four models reduce contamination to single-digit percentages and lift QA F1 by 75–89% relative to WriteAll; on real conversations the reductions span 20% (Scout, MSC-Contam) to 62% (Gemma and Llama-3.3-70B, LoCoMo-Contam), with clean-LoCoMo regression within four points throughout. Llama-3.3-70B is the most reliable verifier (precision =0.998=0.998 across every K∈{1,3,5,10}K{\in}\{1,3,5,10\} and τ∈{0.3,0.5,0.7,0.9}\tau{\in}\{0.3,0.5,0.7,0.9\}, plus the best precision/recall balance on LoCoMo-Contam at Prec =0.810=0.810, Recall =0.680=0.680); Llama4-Scout is the weakest, with its broader soft-score distribution admitting borderline facts at low thresholds (ρ=14.0%\rho{=}14.0\% under the adaptive schedule used here, dropping to 0.30%0.30\% at τ=0.7\tau{=}0.7; Section 6.5). Verifier capability matters but is not a binary requirement: every backbone we tested reduces contamination, and the recommended setting closes most of the cross-model gap.

6.4 Contamination Cascade Effect

Figure 2 traces contamination rate and QA F1 across 100 interaction turns on MemContam. Under WriteAll, contamination stays at 50% and QA F1 saturates at 0.45 as incorrect facts crowd out correct ones in retrieval. Under ConsistencyGate, contamination falls below 3% by turn 90 and QA F1 climbs to 0.88; the gap between the two methods widens monotonically with trajectory length. MemContam’s controlled setting makes this trajectory-level measurement possible; replicating it on real conversations requires turn-level fact labels that current corpora do not provide at scale.

6.5 Ablation Studies

Increasing KK produces only marginal precision gains (1–2 points on Qwen and Gemma between K=1K{=}1 and K=10K{=}10, essentially flat on Scout and Llama-3.3-70B), so we recommend K=5K{=}5 as a conservative default (≤365\leq{}365 ms per fact) and K=1K{=}1 for latency-critical settings. Raising τ\tau from 0.3 to 0.7 sharply improves precision on the three more sensitive backbones (Qwen 0.931→0.9880.931{\to}0.988, Gemma 0.966→0.9840.966{\to}0.984, Scout 0.860→0.9970.860{\to}0.997), and τ=0.9\tau{=}0.9 matches τ=0.7\tau{=}0.7 within noise, identifying τ=0.7\tau{=}0.7 as the natural decision boundary; the adaptive schedule (τmin=0.4,τmax=0.8\tau_{\min}{=}0.4,\tau_{\max}{=}0.8) is a no-tuning fallback that trades roughly five contamination points for one fewer hyperparameter (Qwen: 5.93% vs. 1.19%). Recommended configuration: fixed τ=0.7\tau{=}0.7, K=5K{=}5. The LogProb variant reaches near-perfect precision on MemContam (1.000, 0.984, 0.999, 1.000 across the four backbones) at 23–28 ms per fact, a 12−14×12{-}14\times speedup over K=5K{=}5, but this advantage is specific to structured synthetic contexts; on LoCoMo-Contam soft scoring outperforms LogProb on every backbone (Section 7), so we recommend LogProb only for clean structured source data such as document or tool outputs.

7 Failure Modes and Operating Regime

Operating regime.

ConsistencyGate struggles in two situations. When a candidate fact requires world knowledge beyond what the source context provides, the LLM verifier may consistently vote “yes” for plausible-but-wrong claims (Min et al., 2023); this is the structural limitation that consistency is a proxy for correctness, not correctness itself (§Limitations). When relevant evidence is distributed across many prior conversation turns rather than localized in a single retrievable chunk, the verifier cannot ground its judgment and recall drops (Recall =0.58=0.58 on LoCoMo-Contam versus 1.001.00 on MemContam, §6). The gain is largest in the opposite regime: long trajectories where the cascade has room to compound (Figure 2), and high-recall low-precision writers that leave aggressive extraction for the gate to filter. ConsistencyGate is therefore best suited for document-grounded or tool-grounded memory writes rather than for emergent multi-turn conversational memory.

Context structure moderates LogProb effectiveness.

The single-pass LogProb variant beats soft scoring on MemContam but loses on LoCoMo-Contam on every backbone we tested (Table 5 in Appendix B). This realizes the bimodality asymmetry of §4.2: short structured contexts saturate the yes/no logits so a single forward pass suffices, while long conversational contexts have continuous score distributions that only KK-sample averaging recovers. Use LogProb on clean structured source data (document chunks, tool outputs, knowledge-base entries) and soft scoring on open-ended dialogue.

8 Conclusion

We introduced ConsistencyGate, a write-time self-consistency gate that prevents hallucinated facts from entering LLM agent memory. The gate reduces contamination across two real-conversation benchmarks (LoCoMo-Contam, MSC-Contam) and approaches a near-oracle upper bound on a structured synthetic corpus (MemContam), with no fine-tuning; contamination reductions on real data span 20%–62% across four LLM backbones, with verifier capability emerging as the dominant factor in this spread. The accompanying analysis isolates the contamination cascade: write-time errors compound across long trajectories, so admission decisions made early shape memory quality much later in the interaction. Correctness-based admission is therefore a necessary complement to existing memory management, which has so far focused on utility and capacity. We release code, the benchmarks, and the gate implementation.

Limitations

ConsistencyGate requires LLM access at write time and adds O⁡(K)O(K) cost per fact (the LogProb variant uses one forward pass at 23–28 ms, but only on short structured contexts). Consistency is a proxy for correctness, so ConsistencyGate cannot substitute for authoritative fact-checking. The main deployment risk is implicit-fact recall: the gate rejects 42% of correct probe facts on LoCoMo-Contam (Recall =0.58=0.58, similar across all four backbones), a cost pre-seeding masks here but that is permanent operationally (see §7 for the operating regime in which the gate is applicable).

Broader Impacts

ConsistencyGate aims to make memory-augmented LLM agents more reliable by preventing hallucinated facts from accumulating in long-term memory stores. More reliable agent memory has broad positive applications: agents that assist with medical information retrieval, legal research, or financial planning benefit directly from reduced factual error propagation, and the gains are amplified in exactly the long-horizon settings where these applications operate. Because ConsistencyGate requires no fine-tuning and adds only a write-time check, it is accessible to practitioners deploying existing models without specialized training infrastructure. We also release three benchmarks (MemContam, LoCoMo-Contam, MSC-Contam) so that the community can measure and compare memory contamination methods.

Practitioners should be aware of two deployment-level risks. First, passing a consistency check may create false assurance: end users may treat ConsistencyGate-filtered memory as factually verified when it has only been checked for self-consistency against a potentially unreliable source context. This risk is amplified in high-stakes domains (medical, legal, financial), where practitioners must communicate clearly that consistency filtering is not a substitute for authoritative fact-checking. Second, at deployment scale, K=5K{=}5 calls per fact increases energy consumption; the LogProb variant (≈\approx27 ms, single forward pass) substantially reduces this overhead for latency- or energy-constrained deployments. We do not foresee significant dual-use risks: write-time fact verification does not introduce new capabilities for generating or spreading misinformation.

Appendix D Qualitative Examples

Table 6 shows representative per-fact decisions made by ConsistencyGate on LoCoMo-Contam (Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, K=5K{=}5, soft scoring). Each row shows the extracted fact, the consistency score p^\hat{p}, the adaptive threshold τ∗\tau^{*}, the admission decision, and the ground-truth label.

Analysis.

True positives and true negatives show a clean separation: facts directly supported by memory (e.g., “dancing feels magical”) receive score 1.0, while facts that contradict stored evidence (e.g., “painting” replacing “dancing”) receive score 0.0. False positives arise when the corrupted fact is consistent with but not identical to the correct fact in memory: “Jon and Gina attended a dance class together” is plausible given Gina’s dance class entry, even though the specific corruption was the date. Similarly, “Melanie is into pottery” is supported by memory that lists pottery among several of Melanie’s hobbies, so the gate admits it despite the label counting it as corrupted. False negatives occur when the correct fact is stated indirectly or requires multi-hop inference: “Calvin went to a car show” is correct but the memory stores a longer compound sentence about Dave’s engineering motivation, so the gate cannot directly verify the sub-claim and scores it 0.0. These failure modes motivate future work on multi-hop verification and fine-grained corruption detection.

Appendix E Benchmark Dataset Details

E.1 MemContam

Construction.

MemContam contains 200 samples generated from five synthetic narrative contexts (personal biography, library record, recipe, science fair report, spacecraft mission log). Each context is repeated 200/5=40200/5=40 times with independent LLM-generated fact/corruption sets, giving broad lexical variation despite sharing the same underlying entities. For each sample, Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct is prompted to produce: (i) five correct atomic facts explicitly stated in the context, (ii) five incorrect variants—each derived from a correct fact by entity substitution, number perturbation, negation insertion, or plausible confabulation, and (iii) three question-answer pairs answerable from the correct facts. The dataset thus contains 1,000 correct facts, 1,000 incorrect facts, and 600 QA pairs. By construction, presenting all facts to a WriteAll agent yields exactly ρ=50%\rho=50\% contamination.

Corruption taxonomy.

Incorrect facts are generated via four strategies applied in priority order: (1) Number perturbation: numeric tokens are shifted by a small random delta (e.g., “34-year-old” →\to “35-year-old”); (2) Negation: the first copula is negated (“is” →\to “is not”); (3) Proper-noun substitution: a named entity is replaced with an anonymous placeholder (“MIT” →\to “Another”); (4) Contradicting clause: a “which is incorrect” suffix is appended as a fallback. This taxonomy is designed to produce corruptions that are semantically plausible but factually inconsistent with the source context, the minimal condition for stress-testing a consistency-based gate.

Splits and evaluation.

All 200 samples are used as a single evaluation pool; there is no train split. Experiments use three random seeds (42, 123, 456) that determine the order in which facts are presented to the memory agent. QA metrics (F1, EM) follow the SQuAD normalization: lowercased, punctuation-stripped token overlap.

Source context templates.

The five fixed contexts used to generate all 200 samples are reproduced verbatim below.

  1. 1.

    Personal biography. “Alice Smith is a 34-year-old software engineer at TechCorp who graduated from MIT in 2012. She lives in Seattle with her husband David and their two children, Emma and Jack. Alice enjoys hiking on weekends and has climbed Mount Rainier twice. Her team at TechCorp is working on a new distributed database system called Pegasus.”

  2. 2.

    Library record. “The Westbrook Community Library was founded in 1923 and holds over 80,000 volumes. The current director, Margaret Chen, has been in the role since 2018. The library is open Monday through Saturday, 9am to 8pm, and Sunday 12pm to 5pm. Annual membership costs $25 for adults and $10 for students.”

  3. 3.

    Recipe. “Recipe for Classic Tomato Basil Pasta: Boil 400g of spaghetti for 10 minutes. In a separate pan, sauté 4 cloves of garlic in olive oil for 2 minutes. Add 800g of crushed tomatoes and simmer for 15 minutes. Stir in 30 fresh basil leaves and season with salt and pepper. Serves 4 people. Total preparation time: 35 minutes.”

  4. 4.

    Science fair report. “The 2024 Greenfield Science Fair awarded first place to Sarah Liu, age 15, for her project on photovoltaic efficiency improvements using perovskite coatings. Second place went to Marcus Johnson for his water purification device. The event was held at Lincoln High School on March 12, 2024, with 142 participants.”

    Spacecraft mission log. “The Orion-7 spacecraft launched on June 3, 2023, from Cape Canaveral. It carries a crew of three: Commander Elena Vasquez, Mission Specialist Dr. James Park, and Flight Engineer Priya Nair. The mission duration is planned for 180 days. E.2 LoCoMo-Contam

Source data.

LoCoMo-Contam is derived from LoCoMo-10 (Maharana et al., 2024), a set of 10 long-term dyadic conversations (400–700 turns each, 19–32 sessions per conversation). We use all 10 conversations without filtering.

Probe construction.

For each conversation, we select up to N=5N{=}5 QA pairs from LoCoMo’s annotations, restricting to factual and temporal categories with concrete, verifiable answers. Each QA answer is converted to a self-contained declarative fact using Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct (e.g.,“Caroline moved from Sweden 4 years ago”). A corrupted variant is generated by prompting the model to change exactly one concrete detail (name, number, date, or place) to a plausible but incorrect alternative. Both the correct and corrupted facts are paraphrased into natural conversational utterances as if spoken by one of the conversation participants. The resulting benchmark has 50 probe pairs (5 per conversation) at 50% contamination.

Evaluation protocol.

The agent first processes the full conversation to populate memory. The correct probe facts are then pre-seeded directly into memory (bypassing the gate) to ensure retrieval evidence is always available. The gate is evaluated by presenting each probe turn through the full observe pipeline: the memory writer extracts a fact, the gate queries memory for supporting context, and an admission decision is recorded.

License.

LoCoMo is released under CC BY NC 4.0; our use is non-commercial research only.

E.3 MSC-Contam

Source data.

MSC-Contam is derived from the Multi-Session Chat (MSC) dataset (Xu et al., 2022), comprising 20 dyadic conversations (2 sessions each), grounded in evolving speaker personas. We use all 20 conversations.

Probe construction.

MSC conversations do not provide pre-annotated QA pairs; instead, speakers are given persona sentences at session start. We filter persona sentences for concreteness, keeping only those with a verifiable concrete detail (name, number, place, or occupation), and select up to N=5N{=}5 persona facts per conversation. Each fact is corrupted by changing exactly one concrete detail using the same prompts as LoCoMo-Contam, then paraphrased into a natural conversational utterance. QA pairs for downstream evaluation are generated directly from the original persona facts. The resulting benchmark has 41 probe pairs (up to 5 per conversation ×\times 20 conversations; conversations with fewer than 5 concrete persona facts contribute fewer probes) at 50% contamination.

Evaluation protocol.

Same as LoCoMo-Contam: all session turns are processed to populate memory, correct facts are pre-seeded, and each probe is evaluated through the full gate pipeline.

License.

MSC is released under the MIT License.
